988.title: The hunter on the mountain
988.hook: Arjuna fights a rough mountain hunter and loses, and the hunter turns out to be Shiva
988.carry: shiva lives in everyone, even the hunter
988.howItsDone: At a kirtan, om namah shivaya is sung as a simple call-and-response line, often slowing over many rounds; Shaiva Hindus also repeat it as a mantra in daily japa.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first song of the night, Ganesha's, clearing the road. Honor Ganesha first: he clears the road.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `GANESHA FIRST, CLEARING THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: High in the Himalaya, Arjuna is fasting and praying for weapons before the great war. A boar comes charging at him. He shoots, and at the same moment so does a hunter, a rough mountain man, with a woman at his side. Two arrows, one boar. Whose kill is it? They quarrel. Arjuna, the finest archer alive, starts shooting at the hunter, and his arrows simply vanish into him. His quiver runs empty. He swings his bow, and the hunter snatches it away. They wrestle, and the hero of the Mahabharata is crushed to the ground by a stranger from the hills.
screen: `ONE BOAR, TWO ARROWS.` → `ARJUNA'S ARROWS VANISH.` → `WHO IS THIS HUNTER?`

segments.voice: Beaten, Arjuna does the one thing left. He makes a small altar of earth, honors Shiva there, and lays a garland of flowers on it. Then he looks up. The garland is on the hunter's head. The hunter was Shiva all along, and the woman beside him was the Goddess, Uma. Arjuna falls at his feet, and Shiva, pleased with his courage, gives him the great weapon he came for. The Mahabharata story says what an old hymn says too. The Shri Rudram, in the Krishna Yajur Veda, bows to Rudra, the fierce form of Shiva, over and over, and in places you wouldn't expect: in hunters, potters, carpenters, chariot makers, in forests, fields and streams. It even names the lord of thieves. Inside it are the words that became a famous mantra: namah shivaya, I bow to Shiva, a name that means the kind one, the auspicious one. Om namah shivaya. This is a core Hindu teaching, and Shaivas, the Hindus who worship Shiva as the highest, hold it especially close: the Lord isn't only in the temple. He fills the whole world, and he can turn up as the rough stranger you'd never have guessed. At a kirtan the line goes out fast and comes back slower, round after round. Each round can be a bow to someone different: the person beside you, the one singing off-key, the one you'd rather not sit near. Arjuna learned it flat on the ground; the kirtan teaches it gently.
screen: `THE GARLAND IS ON THE HUNTER'S HEAD.` · `THE HUNTER WAS SHIVA.` · `THE RUDRAM BOWS TO HIM IN EVERYONE.` · `NAMAH SHIVAYA: I BOW TO SHIVA.` · then, large: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA.`

segments.voice: Let the hands rest and the jaw loosen, and on the out-breath say the line silently, or aloud if you're alone: om namah shivaya. Each round, bow inwardly to one person: someone you love, then someone you barely notice, then someone you find hard, the way Arjuna finally bowed to the hunter. If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if not, let it be a way of seeing each one as more than you'd guessed.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: om namah shivaya, I bow to Shiva, the Lord the Rudram finds in everyone, even a hunter on a mountain.

segments.voice: Your line: shiva lives in everyone, even the hunter. Om namah shivaya, a bow to each one. Until tomorrow.

989.title: Rama's name on the tongue
989.hook: a lamp set on the doorstep lights the room and the street at once, and Tulsidas says the tongue is that doorstep
989.carry: rama's name is a lamp on the tongue
989.howItsDone: At kirtan, Shri Ram jai Ram jai jai Ram is sung back and forth, sometimes for a long stretch without changing a word; some Hindus also repeat Rama's name quietly through the day.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: om namah shivaya, and Arjuna's hunter who turned out to be Shiva. Shiva lives in everyone, even the hunter.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `SHIVA LIVES IN EVERYONE, EVEN THE HUNTER.`

segments.voice: One small clay lamp, and evening coming on. Put it inside, and the house is lit but the path outside is dark. Put it out in the lane, and the house goes black. Or set it right on the threshold, the step of the open door, where its light falls both ways at once. Tulsidas, the poet who retold the Ramayana in the language of ordinary people, takes that small household choice and turns it into a teaching about a name: Rama's.
screen: `ONE LAMP, ONE CHOICE.` → `INSIDE, OUTSIDE, OR THE DOORSTEP.` → `TODAY'S SONG: RAMA'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram. Honor to Rama, victory to Rama, victory, victory to Rama. At a kirtan it rocks back and forth like a boat, and some groups sing it for a long time without changing a word. Why only the name? Near the start of the Ramcharitmanas, Tulsidas stops before his story begins and spends a long stretch praising Rama's name. In one couplet he gives the lamp picture, in paraphrase: set the jewel-lamp of Rama's name on the threshold of your tongue, if you want light both inside and outside. The tongue is the doorway between the self and the world, and a name kept there lights both. Then Tulsidas pushes further, and this part can startle. He says the name is, in a way, greater than Rama himself. In the story, Rama freed one woman, Ahalya, the sage's wife who had been turned to stone. The name, Tulsidas says, has turned around the minds of millions. Rama could be in one place at a time. His name can be on every tongue. This is one of the plainest teachings of Hindu devotion: for devotees, the name of God isn't a label for God. God is present in it. It's why many Hindus repeat Rama's name quietly through the day, and why, across much of North India, people still greet each other with Ram Ram. The name needs only a tongue to rest on. That's why the song is so plain. The plainness is the point.
screen: `SHRI RAM, JAI RAM, JAI JAI RAM.` · `A LAMP ON THE TONGUE'S DOORSTEP.` · `RAMA FREED ONE. THE NAME, MILLIONS.` · `GOD IS PRESENT IN THE NAME.` · then, large: `THE PLAINNESS IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Let the mouth relax, lips just touching, and rest your attention on the tongue lying quiet behind the teeth: that's the doorstep. If you pray, set Rama's name there, silently, Ram, Ram, and see whether it lights anything, inside or out; if you'd rather not use the name, rest on that doorway anyway and notice what wants to come out of it today.

990.title: Narada sings, and God comes
990.hook: a song that is nothing but names, and the boy who saw God once and spent his life singing to call him back
990.carry: sing his names and he comes, as if called
990.howItsDone: Krishna devotees sing Govinda jaya jaya and similar strings of names at kirtans and in homes, often speeding up toward a clapping peak and slowing again to a hush.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-NINETY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tulsidas and the lamp. Rama's name is a lamp on the tongue, lighting inside and out.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `RAMA'S NAME, A LAMP ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Govinda jaya jaya, Gopala jaya jaya. Radha Ramana Hari, Govinda jaya jaya. On paper it barely looks like a song. No story, no request, hardly a rhyme. Just names, and the word jaya, victory, hung between them like lanterns on a wire. A kirtan can ride that line up to a fast, clapping peak and then let it fall back to a whisper. Someone hearing it for the first time might ask where the meaning is. It's in the names themselves, and in the story of a boy who became a singing sage.
screen: `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA.` → `NAMES LIKE LANTERNS ON A WIRE.` → `WHERE IS THE MEANING?`

segments.voice: Each name in the song is a small portrait of Krishna. Govinda and Gopala belong to his cowherd years in Vraja. Hari is a name of Vishnu, and devotees honor Krishna as one with Vishnu. Radha Ramana is the one who delights Radha. Now a story about why anyone would sing them. In the Bhagavata Purana, the sage Narada remembers an earlier life. He was a serving woman's little son, who waited on wandering holy men one rainy season and listened as they sang of Hari. Later, left alone, he walked into a forest, sat under a tree and thought of the Lord, and for a moment the Lord appeared in his heart. Then it was gone. A voice told him he wouldn't see that form again in this life; the glimpse was given so he would long for more. So the boy did the one thing left. He went through the world singing the names. And Narada says that ever since, when he sings of the Lord's deeds, the Lord appears quickly in his heart, as if called. The Gita backs him. In chapter nine Krishna describes the great-souled ones, in paraphrase: always singing my glory, striving, firm in their vows, they worship me. The word for singing his glory is kirtayantah, and you can hear kirtan in it. That's the Hindu teaching under every kirtan, nama-sankirtan: the names aren't decoration. For devotees, singing them is a way of calling God, and being heard.
screen: `EACH NAME, A SMALL PORTRAIT.` · `NARADA SAW THE LORD ONCE.` · `SO HE SANG THE NAMES.` · `THE GITA: ALWAYS SINGING MY GLORY.` · then, large: `SING, AND HE COMES AS IF CALLED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a few names you've called out in your life, a parent, a friend, a child, a pet at the door, and notice how each one carries a whole person, and how your voice changes for each. If you pray, take one name of God from your own tradition and say it silently, slowly, the way you'd call someone you hoped would come; if not, rest with the feeling of calling and being called.

991.title: The Goddess in all beings
991.hook: a refrain that never changes, and a list that slips in hunger, sleep and error beside peace and compassion
991.carry: the goddess dwells in all beings, even hunger
991.howItsDone: The ya devi sarva-bhuteshu verses are recited and sung in Goddess worship, especially during Navaratri, and at kirtans the room often joins the unchanging bow while a leader sings the changing word.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-NINETY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Govinda jaya jaya, and Narada's promise. Sing his names and he comes, as if called.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `SING HIS NAMES, AND HE COMES.`

segments.voice: Halfway through the evening, the music changes key and the room turns toward the Goddess. The leader begins a verse with the same ending every time, a run of bows the whole room picks up almost at once. Only one word in the middle changes. Peace. Faith. Compassion. Mother. Words that sound right for a hymn to a goddess. But stay for the whole list, and other words come round too, words nobody would put on a greeting card. Hunger. Sleep. Thirst. And, near the end, error.
screen: `THE ROOM TURNS TO THE GODDESS.` → `ONE WORD CHANGES EACH TIME.` → `PEACE, FAITH ... HUNGER, ERROR.`

segments.voice: The song comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, set inside the Markandeya Purana. In its fifth chapter, two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken over heaven. The gods, thrown out, go to the Himalaya and praise the Goddess. Their verse goes like this in Sanskrit: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, then a quality, rupena samsthita, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. In paraphrase: to the Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of this, bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, bow, bow. Then they fill in the blank. Consciousness. Intelligence. Sleep. Hunger. Power. Thirst. Patience. Peace. Faith. Memory. Compassion. Mother. And error, bhranti, mistaking one thing for another. While they sing, Parvati comes to bathe in the river and asks whom they're praising, and from her own body a goddess steps out and answers: this hymn is for me. Then she goes to face the demons. This is the heart of Shakta teaching, from the Hindus who honor the Goddess as the highest, and many other Hindus share it: Shakti, her power, moves through everything, the bright and the plain alike. She's in the tired body asking for sleep, the stomach asking for food, even the mind that gets it wrong. It's why these verses are chanted at Navaratri, the nine nights of the Goddess. Sung as kirtan, the bow at the end never changes, so even someone with no Sanskrit can join from the second verse. Whatever word comes up, the room bows.
screen: `FROM THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `GODS DRIVEN FROM HEAVEN, SINGING.` · `IN SLEEP, HUNGER, EVEN ERROR.` · `SHAKTI MOVES THROUGH EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `WHATEVER COMES UP, BOW.`

segments.voice: Check in with the body from the stomach up and name what's here, plainly, one word at a time: hunger, tiredness, thirst, restlessness. Then name something brighter that's also here, a little patience, a memory, some contentment, without ranking them, letting each word come and go like the changing word in the hymn. If you pray, follow each word with the hymn's refrain, said silently; if not, notice that both kinds of word belong to the same life.

segments.voice: Late in the evening the drum goes quiet. Someone lights a small flame on a brass plate, a wick in ghee or a piece of camphor, and stands before the image at the front of the room. The plate moves in slow circles while a bell rings in the other hand. The room stands and starts a song some of them clearly know by heart. When the circling stops, the plate is carried through the room. People reach out with both hands, pass their palms over the flame, and draw the warmth back over their eyes and the top of the head.
screen: `THE DRUM GOES QUIET.` → `A FLAME ON A BRASS PLATE.` → `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, TO THE EYES.`

segments.voice: That's aarti: light waved before the deity, often to close a puja or a kirtan. The song sung with it is also called an aarti, and one of the best known in Hindi is Om jai jagdish hare. Its opening, in paraphrase: Om, victory to you, Lord of the world, who removes in a moment the troubles of your devotees. Why offer God a flame at all? An old story answers. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa ends up at the house of Death himself. Death is away, and the boy waits at his door three days without food. Death returns and offers three wishes, and the boy uses the last to ask what happens after we die. Death tries to buy him off with gold and long life. Nachiketa refuses. So Death teaches him, and in that teaching comes a verse, in paraphrase: there the sun doesn't shine, nor moon, nor stars, nor lightning, let alone this little fire. When he shines, everything shines after him; by his light all this is lit. In many temples, especially in the South, that verse is chanted as the camphor flame is waved. Many teachers read the gesture through it: Hindus wave a small flame before the one whose light every light borrows. Then the plate comes round, and people take that light back over their eyes as a blessing. The songs go out. The light comes back.

segments.voice: If there's a candle or a lamp nearby, you can light it, safely; if not, any light will do, even daylight at a window. Hold your palms toward it and feel whatever warmth or brightness reaches them, then slowly bring them back to rest over your closed eyes for a moment. If you pray, let this be your aarti; if not, let it be a moment of receiving something you didn't make.
Kirtan repertoire. The songs a group knows by heart, and the shape they make: from Ganesha at the start to the aarti, the light carried round at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last kirtan song: the aarti, a flame offered to the light behind every light. Everything shines by his light. Now the singing goes quiet, and a book opens.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `EVERYTHING SHINES BY HIS LIGHT.` · `NOW, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Kashi, early morning. A young teacher, already famous for his learning, is walking up from his bath in the Ganga with his students. Coming toward him down the narrow lane is a man of the lowest caste, the kind the society of the day called untouchable, with four dogs at his heels. The teacher does what custom told him to do. Move aside, he says. Get out of the way. The man doesn't move. He asks a question.
screen: `KASHI, AFTER THE MORNING BATH.` → `'MOVE ASIDE.'` → `THE MAN ASKS A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The teacher, tradition says, was Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita, non-duality. And the man's question, as the story is told: what do you want moved away? This body made of food, from that body made of food? Or awareness from awareness? Is the sun any different, reflected in the Ganga or in a puddle in a poor man's lane? Shankara stops. He has taught exactly this: that the one Self, Brahman, is the same in every being. Now a man in the street has shown him that he knew it only as an idea. He bows, and a short poem credited to him says: whoever sees this way, whether outcaste or high-born, is my teacher. Many tellings add that the man was Shiva himself, and the four dogs the four Vedas. That's jnana. Not knowing about, the way you can know the capital of a country you've never seen. Knowing directly, the way you know you're awake. The book we open this week, the Vivekachudamani, the crest-jewel of discernment, also credited to Shankara, warns about this right away. A flood of words and skill in explaining scripture give the learned a kind of enjoyment, it says, but they don't set anyone free. Without realizing the oneness of the Self, there is no freedom. So on this teaching, you can't tell real jnana by what someone can recite. You can tell it by how they treat the person in the lane.
screen: `'BODY FROM BODY, OR SELF FROM SELF?'` · `SHANKARA BOWS.` · `JNANA: KNOWING, NOT KNOWING ABOUT.` · `CLEVER TALK DOESN'T FREE.` · then, large: `ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'll pass today without really seeing: the one who cleans, the driver, the auntie stacking chairs after the program. For a few breaths, set down the labels, the job, the clothes, the place in line, and rest on the plain fact that they're aware, just as you are. That shared awareness is what Shankara's teaching calls the one Self. If you pray, bow inwardly to the Lord in them, as Shankara bowed in the lane; if not, simply notice how the labels loosen.
Jnana. Knowing, the direct kind, not knowing about. In Shankara's story it's the knowing that sees one Self in the man in the lane, which no amount of clever talk can stand in for.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shankara bowing to the man in the lane. Jnana is knowing the one self in everyone. This week ran from Ganesha, Shiva, Rama, Govinda, the Goddess and the aarti into a quiet book.
screen: `JNANA.` · `ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.` · `A WEEK FROM SONG TO SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Kashi again. Shankara is walking by when he hears an old man drilling himself on Sanskrit grammar, the same rule over and over, dukrin karane, dukrin karane, as if his life depended on it. The man is near the end of his life, and still memorizing. And Shankara, the great teacher of knowing, doesn't hand him an argument. Tradition says he sings to him. The song begins: Bhaja Govindam. Worship Govinda.
screen: `AN OLD MAN CRAMMING GRAMMAR.` → `SHANKARA DOESN'T ARGUE.` → `HE SINGS: BHAJA GOVINDAM.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in paraphrase: worship Govinda, worship Govinda, worship Govinda, foolish mind. When your time comes, the grammar rule won't save you. That's Govinda from our kirtan four days ago, Krishna's cowherd name, on the lips of the philosopher of knowing. The Vivekachudamani, also credited to Shankara, shows why that's no contradiction. It names four things a seeker needs: viveka, discernment between the lasting and the passing; vairagya, letting go of the hunger for enjoyments; six treasures, among them calm, restraint, endurance and faith; and the longing to be free. If letting go and longing are weak, it says, the rest are like mirages in a desert. Then the surprise, in paraphrase: among all the means to freedom, bhakti, devotion, is the greatest. And bhakti, the text says, is the seeking of one's own true nature. Hindus often speak of jnana and bhakti, knowing and loving, as two paths. Here they meet. Shankara's tradition credits him with both the hard arguments and the hymns. The old scholar's mistake wasn't studying. It was mistaking the rule for the goal. To love the truth of who you are enough to keep looking for it: on this reading, that's bhakti, and it's what the singing and the book were both for.
screen: `BHAJA GOVINDAM: WORSHIP GOVINDA.` · `DISCERNMENT, LETTING GO, SIX TREASURES, LONGING.` · `BHAKTI IS THE GREATEST MEANS.` · `BHAKTI: SEEKING YOUR OWN NATURE.` · then, large: `KNOWING AND LOVING MEET.`

segments.voice: Let the eyes close and sort your day so far into two piles: things that were passing, a mood, a headline, a craving, a small worry, and anything that seemed to stay. Don't argue about which pile something goes in; just practice the sorting, which is viveka in a small way. If you pray, say Govinda's name once, softly, as Shankara sang it to the old scholar; if not, hold the longing to know what lasts.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it rests on discernment, letting go and longing, and the text calls the seeking of your own nature bhakti.

segments.voice: Your line: jnana and bhakti, knowing and loving, meet. Even the road of knowing runs on love. That's day nine hundred ninety-four.
